item.title: Sharp Instrumental Variable Bounds under The Marginal Sensitivity Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.22513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Marginal sensitivity models bound the degree of unmeasured confounding but do not incorporate instrumental-variable restrictions, even when an instrument is available. We develop a framework combining these models with instrumental-variable assumptions to sharpen inference on population treatment effects without requiring treatment monotonicity or treatment-effect homogeneity. For continuous and finite ordered outcomes, we characterize sharp identified sets for potential-outcome means and the average treatment effect, together with observable restrictions implied jointly by the instrumental-variable and sensitivity assumptions. The bounds admit explicit formulas for finite ordered outcomes, while optimization over prespecified threshold classes provides tractable outer bounds for continuous outcomes. We develop cross-fitted one-step estimators that accommodate flexible nuisance estimation. Under suitable conditions, the resulting outward confidence sets asymptotically cover the sharp identified interval without requiring optimal threshold estimation. Stronger conditions yield semiparametric efficient estimation and inference for restricted-class bounds. Numerical experiments show narrower confidence sets when incorporating an instrument and compare the performance of outward inference and inference for individual bounds. We apply the framework to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment to illustrate how combining instrumental-variable assumptions with restrictions on the degree of unmeasured confounding can strengthen conclusions about the effect of Medicaid coverage on emergency-department use.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Olivas-Martinez, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen

item.title: Goodness-of-Fit Tests via Kernel Density Estimation: Univariate and Multivariate Approaches
item.description: arXiv:2610.22541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces goodness-of-fit tests based on leave-one-out kernel density estimation (KDE) for both univariate and multivariate data. The proposed test statistic takes the form of a log-likelihood ratio comparing a parametric null model with a nonparametric KDE-based estimator, where the leave-one-out construction removes the in-sample bias inherent in standard kernel density estimators. For univariate densities with bounded support, boundary bias is mitigated via reflection techniques. We establish consistency of the proposed tests and show that, under fixed alternatives, the normalized log-statistic converges to the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the true density and the closest parametric model under the null, providing an information-theoretic interpretation of the procedure. A parametric bootstrap is used for finite-sample calibration. Extensive simulation studies and real data applications demonstrate strong empirical performance across a range of univariate and multivariate settings, including heavy-tailed, skewed, and multimodal alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Luai Al-Labadi, Ayman Alzaatreh, Ruodie Yu, Kairui Bao

item.title: A Bayesian hierarchical model for preferentially sampled spatial extremes data: an application to air quality
item.description: arXiv:2610.22577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) establish concentration limits for criteria pollutants in order to safeguard public health and the environment. For some NAAQS, the standard refers to thresholds for either high percentiles or maxima. Identifying regions where regulatory thresholds are exceeded involves using geostatistical models, often formulated under the implicit assumption that observations arise from locations randomly sampled in the spatial domain. However, this does not hold for air pollution monitors as they are often preferentially placed in areas with elevated extreme concentration levels. Using the yearly maximum concentration of PM2.5 as a case study, we investigate whether preferential sampling affects inference and prediction for spatial extremes. To this goal, we propose a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounts for preferential sampling by introducing a shared latent, spatial process that informs both the median of the blended Generalized Extreme Value (bGEV) distribution and the probability that a site is selected to be a sampling location. Application of the proposed model to simulated data reveals that, not accounting for preferential sampling, results in systematic biases in parameters estimates, whereas application to observations of yearly maxima PM2.5 concentrations in California between 2017 and 2024 shows that not accounting for preferential sampling can significantly alter conclusions about exceedance regions.
item.dc:creator: Bianca Brusco Veronica J. Berrocal

item.title: Proximal Causal Inference for Time Series from N-of-1Mobile Device Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.22647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unmeasured confounding challenges causal inference in intensive longitudinal studies, potentially biasing treatment effect estimates. The proximal causal inference (PCI) framework offers a promising approach to identification using proxies or negative control variables in the presence of hidden confounding bias. While prior literature considers the joint effect of time-varying treatments, our work extends the framework to a time series setting to estimate the contemporaneous or lagged effect of time-varying treatments. We demonstrate that under traditional PCI assumptions, we can recover unbiased effect estimation in the presence of unmeasured confounding by leveraging the intensive longitudinal nature of time series data. Specifically, we develop identifiability conditions and show that past and future observations can be employed as natural proxies for unmeasured confounders. We further develop the bridge function required for valid PCI estimation along with asymptotic variance. Simulation studies illustrate our method's validity and robustness to violation of certain PCI identification assumptions. We demonstrate the potential for studying socio-environmental exposure health effects by applying our method to a smartphone study of bipolar patients. Our work contributes to the growing literature on PCI and provides a powerful tool for analyzing longitudinal data, including in observational mobile health research prone to confounding bias.
item.dc:creator: Fanyu Cui, Charlotte Fowler, Xiaoxuan Cai, Jukka-Pekka Onnela, Justin Baker, Linda Valeri

item.title: Robust Estimation under Spurious Correlation via Statistical Counterfactual Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2610.22649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spurious correlations between nuisance features and outcomes present a fundamental challenge for statistical learning and inference. Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), the practice of resampling nuisance features while preserving features of interest, has emerged as a popular strategy to mitigate such correlations, yet its statistical properties, and its reliance on an untestable validity assumption, remain largely unexplored. We provide a statistical treatment of CDA, termed Statistical CDA (SCDA), with two components. First, casting SCDA as a simulated-moment M-estimator, we establish consistency, asymptotic normality with a sandwich covariance and a finite-augmentation-draw variance correction, oracle efficiency for the target parameter, and the equivalence of iterative and one-shot procedures via stochastic approximation, yielding valid large-sample inference where previously none was available. Second, because the augmentation's validity cannot be tested from the observed data when features are entangled (a fact we prove), we develop a sensitivity analysis that bounds the residual nuisance--outcome dependence by a parameter $\Gamma$, giving sharp identified intervals for the target with valid confidence intervals and a breakdown frontier; the point-identified theory is the $\Gamma=0$ special case. Simulations confirm the efficiency gains under validity and the robustness bounds under possible invalidity, placing a widely used augmentation method on a transparent inferential footing.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Hui Zhou, George Sun

item.title: A Bayesian Hidden Markov Model with Singh--Maddala Emission Distributions for Heavy-Tailed Regime-Switching Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.22656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heavy-tailed time series with regime switching arise in environmental, financial, and engineering applications, yet conventional emission distributions such as Gaussian, Gamma, or Weibull fail to capture simultaneously extreme right-skewness, slowly decaying upper tails, and temporal dependence. This paper develops a fully Bayesian Hidden Markov Model with Singh-Maddala (Burr Type XII) emission distributions (HMMSM). We derive the complete Bayesian structure and design an adaptive Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler combining Forward-Filtering Backward-Sampling, conjugate Dirichlet updates, and adaptive Metropolis steps. Simulations confirm parameter recovery with relative errors below 10% and 95% prediction coverage of 94.5%. On a simulated benchmark with heavy tails, Bayesian model selection via WAIC, DIC, and LOO correctly identifies K = 3, and HMMSM outperforms seven competing specifications by large margins. On a 26-year gridded rainfall record for Ireland (T = 312 monthly observations), HMMSM attains the lowest WAIC but is statistically indistinguishable from HMM-Gamma, reflecting the light tails of Irish rainfall. The selected two-regime model identifies a Moderate regime (mean approx. 87 mm) and a Wet regime (approx. 134 mm) that are persistent and seasonally coherent. We also document weak identifiability of the Singh-Maddala scale parameter. The framework is general-purpose, and reproducible code is provided.
item.dc:creator: Safaa K. Kadhem

item.title: Borrowing Space, Clustering Temporal Dynamics: Bayesian Regime Mapping and Spatial Prediction for European PM10
item.description: arXiv:2610.22699v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Daily particulate matter measurements from European monitoring networks vary both through spatially shared fluctuations and through differences in local temporal dynamics. Characterising both features is important for identifying groups of monitoring locations with similar temporal behaviour and for predicting concentrations at unmonitored sites. We develop a Bayesian model that combines a continuous spatial common-shock process with a spatial product partition prior for clustering locations according to their local persistence and innovation variability. At unmonitored locations, the model extends these components through spatial interpolation and probabilistic regime allocation. Sparse spatial computations and online prediction summaries make inference feasible for 2,989 monitoring locations and 5,297 unmonitored land locations over 2024. Replicated simulations show that geographic information improves recovery of weakly separated, spatially organised regimes, while uncertainty in regime allocation need not prevent useful continuous prediction. The European analysis identifies stable clusters spanning national boundaries. Clusters with similar persistence nevertheless differ in local innovation variability and in how consistently their stations are grouped together across posterior draws. Comparisons with three restricted models clarify the complementary roles of spatially shared variation, heterogeneous local dynamics and geographic information in the partition.
item.dc:creator: Luca Aiello, Lucia Clarotto

item.title: Negative-binomial ensemble filtering for discrete-time Hawkes network reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2610.22742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a sequential ensemble filter for reconstructing directed excitation networks from overdispersed multivariate counts observed on a regular time grid. The data-generating model is a discrete-time negative-binomial Hawkes process, for which we prove exact first- and second-moment stability conditions and derive a row-wise sufficient condition. The filter learns the network and the dispersion online, and a row-composition parameter forecast keeps enough ensemble variation to respond to structural change. In synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that a Poisson-based filter provides comparable point-estimate accuracy of the network, while the proposed filter provides substantially better calibrated predictive and parameter uncertainty. Under an abrupt redistribution of influence, the filter recovers connections that are absent before the change. An application to daily property-crime counts in sixteen Chicago community areas gives broadly calibrated one-step predictions and a recovered network consistent with independent temporal and geographic information.
item.dc:creator: Naratip Santitissadeekorn

item.title: Pattern Graph Models for Non-monotone Missing Data with an Application to Myocardial Infarction Complications
item.description: arXiv:2610.22757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-monotone missingness is frequently encountered in practice, with intermittent dropout and re-entry in longitudinal studies as a canonical example. Under non-monotone missingness, the missing at random (MAR) assumption often lacks a clear causal interpretation and imposes implicit constraints on the joint distribution that may be difficult to justify. Within the pattern graph framework, we propose a fully parametric estimation procedure that combines pattern-graph-identified response probabilities with a parametric outcome model through an EM algorithm with fractional imputation. Under correct model specification and explicit regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality when the fractional imputation is exact or sufficiently accurate, and, under additional moment conditions, justify parametric bootstrap variance estimation. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed approach is competitive across a range of settings and provides substantial efficiency gains for joint probability estimation when fully observed cases are scarce. The methods are illustrated through an analysis of mortality risk factors in data on myocardial infarction complications.
item.dc:creator: Yanghyeon Cho, Jae Kwang Kim, Emily Berg

item.title: Optimal subsampling approach for Cox models under large-scale length-biased right-censored data
item.description: arXiv:2610.22793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid advancement of data acquisition technologies, massive survival data have become increasingly prevalent, posing substantial computational challenges for the standard Cox proportional hazards model under complex censoring and truncation mechanisms. This paper addresses the analysis of large-scale length-biased right-censored data within the Cox model framework. We propose a novel subsampling approach to enhance computational efficiency for large samples and establish theoretically that the resulting subsample estimator provides an efficient approximation to the full-data estimator, while preserving consistency and asymptotic normality. Explicit optimal subsampling probabilities are derived under A- and L-optimality criteria. To facilitate practical implementation, we develop an efficient two-step estimation algorithm. Extensive numerical simulations and an empirical analysis of U.S. airline flight operation data evaluate the estimation performance and computational gains under various censoring rates and sample sizes. The results demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces computational cost while preserving statistical accuracy, offering a practical and scalable solution for analyzing large-scale length-biased right-censored survival data.
item.dc:creator: Zhicheng Feng, Panpan Ba, Jianhua Shi, Lin Ouyang

item.title: Joint Estimation and Feature Selection in Overspecified Finite Mixture of Regressions
item.description: arXiv:2610.22851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate joint estimation and feature selection in sparse finite mixtures of regressions with an overspecified number of mixture components or mixture order. More specifically, given a conservative fixed upper bound on the unknown mixture order, we deliberately overspecify the order and propose a double-penalized likelihood approach for simultaneous parameter estimation and feature selection. We establish consistent recovery of the sparsity structure of the underlying mixing measure in terms of its regression coefficients, showing that the true sparsity of the mixture regression can be consistently identified even under order over-specification. The proposed methodology incorporates two complementary penalties: the first penalizes small (near-zero) mixing proportions, inducing an asymptotic Voronoi-type partition of the estimated regression vectors into clusters associated with the true sparse regression vectors; the second penalizes regression coefficients, resulting in sparsity through the selection of relevant features. Although the sparsity penalty is applied to individual regression coefficients, the combined effect of the two penalties yields an asymptotic group feature selection property where the same features tend to be selected or not selected within each Voronoi cluster. We develop a modified EM algorithm combined with proximal gradient for numerical implementations. Extensive simulations and a real data application demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
item.dc:creator: Abbas Khalili, Pengqi Liu, Huy Nguyen, Nhat Ho

item.title: Sparsity-Corrected Tensor Clustering for Multi-Layer Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.22859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-layer networks provide complementary views of interactions among the same set of nodes. In practice, layers with similar community structures may have substantially different network sparsity, causing sparsity variation to obscure the structural patterns of interest. To address this problem, a sparsity heterogeneous mixture multi-layer stochastic block model is proposed, which separates layer-specific sparsity from group-specific community structure. Based on the induced low-rank tensor representation, a sparsity-corrected tensor clustering method is proposed to remove the layer-specific scale effect before clustering, without explicitly estimating the sparsity parameters. Theoretical guarantees for tensor decomposition, layer clustering, and community detection are established. The results further characterize the range of sparsity heterogeneity allowed for consistent recovery, including regimes where the sparsity ratio diverges with the network dimensions. Numerical studies and an application to international trade networks from BACI demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method under heterogeneous layer sparsity.
item.dc:creator: Xuefei Wang, Gaorong Li, Wenyang Zhang

item.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
item.description: arXiv:2610.22930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.
item.dc:creator: Junyu Cao, Ruijiang Gao, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky, Mingzhang Yin

item.title: Online Conditional Vine Copulas: Forecasting Electricity Demand
item.description: arXiv:2610.23119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an online multivariate distributional forecasting model in which we condition the parameters of a vine copula on covariates. An online algorithm updates the parameters sequentially using only the most recent observations. Existing approaches require full batch re-estimation using all available data at each update step, which makes them computationally slow in large-scale forecasting applications and less suitable for settings in which dependence structures change over time. Simulation results show that the online procedure achieves forecasting performance comparable to that of the batch estimator, while reducing computation time substantially. We illustrate the method in a forecasting application to electricity net-demand across five regions of Great Britain and show that (i) the conditional vine copula model outperforms unconditional Gaussian and vine copula benchmarks and (ii) that online estimation improves forecast accuracy when batch re-estimation is not available. The algorithm is implemented in the Python package ondil.
item.dc:creator: Christian Jobelius Schulz, Christoph Hanck, Simon Hirsch, Florian Ziel

item.title: Testing Treatment Effect Heterogeneity with Functional Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.23397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assessing treatment-effect heterogeneity is important in causal inference, particularly for functional outcomes where effects may vary over time and the common effect is unknown. We propose a nonparametric procedure that assesses treatment-effect homogeneity through a testable marginal implication. By comparing within-arm difference distributions, the construction removes the unknown common functional effect without estimating it. We measure departures between these distributions through an integrated squared discrepancy of their characteristic functionals. A full-support Gaussian integrating measure yields an explicit bounded-kernel representation and identifies equality of the difference laws without requiring moment conditions on the outcomes. We construct an unbiased generalized U-statistic that accounts for dependence among overlapping differences, derive its null, fixed-alternative, and local-alternative limits, and develop a centered multiplier bootstrap for inference. The framework extends to multiple treatment arms with a shared control. For computation, a random-direction approximation combined with a nine-state recursion reduces the cost to linear order in the sample size for fixed numerical settings. Simulation studies assess the finite-sample performance of the proposed procedure relative to several benchmark methods. An application to the Irish gas smart-metering trial illustrates its use for assessing heterogeneity in functional treatment responses.
item.dc:creator: Yongzhen Feng, Jie Li, Xiaojun Song

item.title: Closely spaced change-point detection with an application to geopolitical shocks in oil and gas markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.23476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Change points that arrive in quick succession, or near the boundaries of the sample, are prone to type-II error: the few observations trapped between successive breaks carry too little information for global procedures to analyze. This article develops a test statistic, $I_1$, for which we derive the limiting null distribution under Gaussian noise, extend the theory to weakly dependent sequences, and prove consistency under a mean-shift alternative. Around $I_1$, we construct DCI, a two-phase algorithm that couples a global scan with multiple local tests via an adaptive-width sliding window. In extensive simulations, $I_1$ and DCI remain Pareto-optimal over criteria spaces spanning true and false positive rates, localization error, and segmentation covering. An application to the US-Iran 2026 conflict quantifies the exposure of energy markets to geopolitical shocks using two new metrics, event sensitivity and event attribution, leading to time series tokenization.
item.dc:creator: Nachiketas Waychal, Arnab Kumar Laha, Ankur Sinha

item.title: Scaling Spatially Varying Distributed Lag Nonlinear Models for Nationwide Small-Area Data: A Divide-and-Conquer Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.23501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lagged and nonlinear exposure-response relationships are frequently modelled using distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs). However, these relationships can vary substantially across locations due to differences in climate, population structure, adaptation and socio-economic characteristics, among others. Spatially-varying DLNMs can capture this heterogeneity, but their computational demands limit their application to fine-scale nationwide datasets with thousands of small areas. In this paper, we adapt a 'divide-and-conquer' approach to spatially varying DLNMs. The method partitions the spatial domain into smaller regions, expands each region with a k-order neighbourhood to reduce boundary effects, fits separate models within each partition using Laplacian P-splines, and combines the resulting estimates using conditional predictive ordinate-based mixture weights. We evaluated the approach in a simulation study based on municipalities in Sicily and applied it to daily summer temperature and mortality data from 7122 municipalities in mainland Italy between 2011 and 2021. Simulation studies show good performance, with relative-risk estimates comparable to those from a global model and relatively robust to the choice and number of partitioning units. Computational efficiency can be substantially improved by using parallel computations. The Italian application reveals significant spatial heterogeneity in the temperature-mortality relationship, with clear regional differences. The proposed framework makes spatially varying DLNMs feasible for large, fine-scale spatiotemporal datasets while retaining location-specific exposure-lag-response estimation.
item.dc:creator: Sara Rutten, Thomas Neyens, Elisa Duarte, Christel Faes

item.title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.
item.dc:creator: Yang Ni

item.title: A Bayesian model averaging approach for estimating longitudinal treatment effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.23578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several methods have been proposed for performing variable selection for the goal of estimating the average treatment effect of a point treatment on an outcome. Much less work has focused on developing methods for performing variable selection when the goal is instead to estimate the causal effect of a longitudinal treatment on an outcome. We introduce a Bayesian model averaging approach to estimate counterfactual means under longitudinal treatment regimes as well as the parameters of longitudinal marginal structural models. The Bayesian model averaging framework provides a principled way to produce valid post-selection inference. We further devise an informative prior distribution that favors the selection of optimal adjustment sets, in the sense that the resulting estimator has the lowest possible variance among all possible adjustment sets. We show through simulation results that our proposed method outperforms fully adjusted estimators and even performs similarly to an oracle estimator in several scenarios. In a real-data illustration, our method yields estimates with markedly reduced standard errors for the effect of cumulative exposure to statins for the prevention of a first cardiovascular disease or death among older adults.
item.dc:creator: David Adenyo, Mireille E. Schnitzer, Jason R. Guertin, Denis Talbot

item.title: Efficient spectral unmixing using endmember variability
item.description: arXiv:2610.23793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A mixed signal vector composed of a weighted sum of random, unobserved endmember vectors has a mean and a variance that both depend on the unknown weights. This suggests that linear estimates of the weights based on the mean model are likely to be inefficient, and could possibly be improved upon by estimates that also make use of the variance model. In the context of a latent factor model for source variability, we calculate theoretically how much information is available in the variance model, and show how this information may stabilize inference in the case of an ill-conditioned mean model. We show through several data examples that utilization of the variance model is likely to improve parameter estimation in real-world scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Jordan Bryan, Peter Hoff, Galen Reeves

item.title: Source-Aware Dynamic Pricing with Strategic Buyers
item.description: arXiv:2610.22516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In modern commerce, firms and platforms typically use customer features from different sources to personalize prices: some features are verified using seller records or third-party data, while others are self-reported and may be strategically manipulated by buyers seeking lower prices. We therefore introduce a novel source-aware framework for contextual dynamic pricing with strategic buyers in a high-dimensional semiparametric setting, where buyer valuations follow a sparse linear model with an unknown noise distribution. To account for differences in manipulability across feature sources while enabling effective valuation learning, we develop the Source-Aware Localized exploration and calibrated Exploitation (SALE) pricing policy, which draws on verified features to localize price exploration and combines verified and reported features to correct for strategic manipulation during exploitation. Our localized exploration design allows converting binary purchase feedback into unbiased signals of conditional mean valuations, yielding a new population equation that supports consistent sparse estimation despite non-i.i.d. buyer arrivals. Building on this estimate, we develop a localized empirical-process analysis that exploits intrinsic sparse geometry to establish uniform guarantees for nonparametric estimation of the noise distribution in the high-dimensional setting. With these estimation guarantees, we establish SALE's self-recovery property, which keeps localized exploration valid with high probability and leads to a sublinear expected regret bound. Both simulation studies and real-data experiments demonstrate the appealing performance of SALE. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to provide a theoretical and practical framework for incorporating information provenance into dynamic pricing with strategic buyers.
item.dc:creator: Jinjiang Zou, Yang Li, Zemin Zheng

item.title: On strongly coherent confidence envelopes for the false discoveries
item.description: arXiv:2610.22601v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coherence is a long term notion in the literature of multiple testing. From FWER control multiple testing theory to confidence envelopes on the number of false positives, coherence is a desirable property for multiple testing procedures. However, we show in this article that coherence is not a sufficient property to ensure that a multiple testing procedure is nonimprovable via an interpolation mechanism. We introduce a new no- tion, the notion of strong coherence, which is a stronger property than coherence and ensures that a multiple testing procedure is nonimprovable via the interpolation mech- anisms considered in the literature. Finally, we provide a uniform improvement of the confidence envelope from Durand et al. (2020) that is computable in polynomial time and demonstrate the improvement on simulated data.
item.dc:creator: Romain P\'erier, Gilles Blanchard, Guillermo Durand

item.title: Weighted spatial averages with missing observations: Convergence and accuracy of delta-method variance approximations
item.description: arXiv:2610.23504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weighted spatial averages from incomplete networks are ratios whose variance is approximated by truncating a Taylor series (the delta method). Three questions remain open: whether the series converges, how large a truncation's error is, and how it behaves as the network grows. We address these for observations missing completely at random, independently with a common probability $\alpha$. First, the truncations, which count corrections for the denominator (the total reported weight) and for its coupling with the numerator, converge for a given network only if $\alpha>\tfrac12$ and both corrections increase together. Second, whether or not the series converges, the error of truncations correcting only for the denominator is controlled at any network size by its coefficient of variation $\rho$, with $\rho^2=\tfrac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\sum_i\beta_i^2$ for weights $\beta_i$, and by the probability of rare reporting patterns. Third, for uniform weights and bounded fields, these errors vanish as the network grows, at any fixed availability. If correlations also decay with distance, the first-order approximation of earlier work has error of order $\rho^4$, against $\rho^2$ for the simplest approximation. Only truncations of equal order in numerator and denominator, beginning with the first-order truncation, avoid spurious dependence on the mean level; higher ones need not be more accurate. The exact variance for uniform weights, a single sum, shows that for correlated fields the first-order approximation overstates the contribution of missing data but is conservative overall. Concentrated weights degrade it more than $\rho$ indicates. Rainfall simulations over India illustrates results, several of which extend to self-normalized estimators.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin K Seshadri, Abhishek Pal Majumder

item.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.23570v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent work has constructed anytime-valid envelopes that do, but deterministic envelopes are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each coupling a specific algorithm to a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for constructing such anytime-valid data-adaptive boundaries for a large class of iterative algorithms. Performance measures of many of these algorithms satisfy a one-step recursion that reduces the entire error analysis to a single general requirement: time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. We formalize this through a strongly adapted sub-$\psi$ condition, and derive off-the-shelf boundary constructions via continuous and discrete mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. We show how these boundaries can be directly coupled with a separate algorithmic analysis that derives the one-step recursion to provide a class of readymade anytime-valid envelopes across diverse settings including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), temporal difference learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD. In particular, for SGD, our framework either recovers or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Soham Bonnerjee, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Robust Local Fr\'echet Regression: Nonasymptotic Theory and Minimax Optimality
item.description: arXiv:2610.23757v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop robust local Fr\'echet regression for heavy-tailed responses in a general metric space and propose a distance-based median-of-means estimator. We derive nonasymptotic pointwise high-probability bounds separately under local second-order smoothness and local $1$-Wasserstein H\"older continuity, and show that the corresponding optimized rates match the classical pointwise rates for nonparametric regression. We also establish matching pointwise minimax lower bounds over embedded Gaussian regression subclasses. Remarkably, our results do not require an entropy condition on the response space. Simulation studies with positive-definite matrix-valued responses, together with a real-data application involving Wasserstein-valued responses, illustrate the robustness--efficiency tradeoff and practical performance of the proposed estimator.
item.dc:creator: Chang Jun Im, Daisuke Kurisu

item.title: Canonical Layer Inference for Deep Gaussian Processes via Symmetry-Breaking Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2610.23842v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible priors for compositional regression functions, but inference for intermediate layers faces questions. The basic obstruction is an adjacent-layer symmetry: applying an invertible transformation and its inverse to two adjacent layers leaves the composed regression map unchanged. Under explicit symmetry and prior-comparability conditions, we show that the posterior may not concentrate on any prescribed intermediate-layer representation, even when the composed regression function is estimable. We then introduce an augmented $\rho$-fractional posterior that reweights layer decompositions by a non-saturating identity-deviation penalty. The augmentation changes posterior odds between symmetry-related decompositions by an exponential penalty ratio. Under proper choices of the penalty and a prior mass condition, it preserves function-level fractional posterior contraction, while shrinking the redundant layers towards the identity mapping. Thus, the likelihood does not identify a unique ``true'' set of layers; the augmentation favors identity-biased parsimonious decompositions within an equivalence class of layers; uniqueness of a selected representative is not established.
item.dc:creator: Yichen Zhu, Hengrui Luo

item.title: Learning Joint Graphical Model with Computational Efficiency, Dynamic Regularization, and Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2503.18722v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-sourced datasets are common in studies of variable interactions, for example, heterogeneous gene networks, cross-domain recommendation, etc., where each source induces a related but distinct dependency structure. Joint learning of multiple graphical models (i.e., multiple precision matrices) has emerged as an important tool in analyzing such data. Unlike separate learning, joint learning can leverage shared structural patterns across graphs to yield more accurate results. In this paper, we present an adaptive method named MIGHT (Multi-task Iterative Graphical Hard Thresholding) to estimate multiple graphs jointly. We introduce an $\ell_0$-based similarity measure, reformulate the joint model as a series of multi-task learning problems, and solve them using a dynamically regularized algorithm based on iterative hard thresholding. By leveraging the efficiency of the iterative procedure and the inherent parallelizability of the nodewise framework, the proposed method is computationally efficient and amenable to parallel implementation. Theoretically, we derive the non-asymptotic error bound for the resulting estimator under joint Gaussian graphical models. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is adaptive to heterogeneous column-wise signal strengths: for nodes with strong signals, our estimator achieves improved error bounds and selection consistency adaptively, and also exhibits asymptotic normality without an additional debiasing step. The performance of our method is illustrated through numerical simulations and real-data analysis on a cancer gene-expression RNA-seq dataset.
item.dc:creator: Shixiang Liu, Yanhang Zhang, Zhifan Li, Jianxin Yin

item.title: Closed-form Covariance Functions in Space and Time from B-spline Spectral Densities
item.description: arXiv:2506.21953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The autocovariance function (ACF) is central to the analysis of time series, spatial, and spatio-temporal data. Classical parametric models are often too restrictive for multivariate and space-time data, which motivates non-parametric descriptions of the ACF. Bochner's Theorem guarantees that any positive spectral measure yields a valid ACF via the inverse Fourier transform; however, existing non-parametric approaches in the spectral domain rarely return closed-form expressions for the ACF itself. We develop a closed-form class of non-parametric ACFs by deriving the inverse Fourier transform of B-spline spectral bases with arbitrary degree and knot placement. This yields a family of closed-form stationary covariance models with three properties: (i) it is uniformly dense for the ACF, among the ACFs of weakly stationary processes that possess a spectral density; (ii) it accommodates univariate, multivariate, and multidimensional processes; and (iii) it is non-separable in general, with separability a special case. Jackson-type approximation bounds establish convergence rates, and simulation studies show accurate recovery of known univariate and bivariate ACFs. Applied to output from a high-resolution ocean simulation, the fit space-time ACF is non-separable and demonstrates accurate process recovery.
item.dc:creator: Lachlan Astfalck

item.title: Measuring frailty in older adults: an indicator based on a super-classifier
item.description: arXiv:2506.22349v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Identifying frail older adults in an ageing population is essential for improving healthcare services. This study proposes a composite indicator to assess individual frailty levels using administrative healthcare data. Given the complex and multidimensional nature of frailty, a multi-outcome approach is adopted. Following an extensive literature review, a set of adverse health events is selected as proxies for frailty. These events were modelled using logistic classifiers, with frailty determinants (associated to adverse health events, selected using a gradient tree boosting) serving as covariates. The sensitivity and specificity of each classifier is used to compose their combined likelihood. From this, we derive an indicator capable of quantifying frailty across the population. The indicator shows robust performance across multiple outcomes and over time. Its primary innovation lies in allowing the use of diverse and outcome-specific sets of frailty determinants without any structural constraint. Overall, we offer an effective tool for quantifying frailty among older adults, potentially supporting health authorities in the prevention of frailty-related adverse events.
item.dc:creator: Sara Rebottini, Margherita Silan, Pietro Belloni

item.title: Stabilizing Thompson Sampling with Null Hypothesis Bayesian Response-Adaptive Randomization
item.description: arXiv:2510.01734v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Response-adaptive randomization (RAR) methods can be used to adapt randomization probabilities based on accumulating data, aiming to increase the probability of allocating patients to effective treatments. A popular RAR method is Thompson sampling, which randomizes patients proportionally to the Bayesian posterior probability that each treatment is the most effective. However, its high variability can also increase the risk of assigning patients to inferior treatments and lead to inferential problems such as confidence interval undercoverage. We propose a principled method based on Bayesian hypothesis testing to address these issues: We introduce a null hypothesis postulating equal effectiveness of treatments. Bayesian model averaging then induces shrinkage toward equal randomization probabilities, with the degree of shrinkage controlled by the prior probability of the null hypothesis. Equal randomization and Thompson sampling arise as special cases when the prior probability is one or zero, respectively. A simulation study demonstrates that the method can mitigate issues with Thompson sampling and has comparable statistical properties to Thompson sampling with common ad hoc modifications such as power transformation and probability capping. Under the null hypothesis and a normal model, the randomization probabilities are shown to converge asymptotically to equal randomization, unlike those of Thompson sampling. We implement the method in the free and open-source R package brar, enabling experimenters to easily perform null hypothesis Bayesian RAR and support more effective randomization of patients.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Pawel, Leonhard Held

item.title: Heterogeneity-adaptive shrinkage estimation and inference for linear panel models
item.description: arXiv:2603.10918v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent shrinkage estimators for linear panel models have focused on increasing flexibility beyond empirical Bayes estimators to deliver mean squared error optimality, but these estimators' performance rarely meets their theoretical guarantees in practice. To balance theoretical and practical performance, we develop a heterogeneity-adaptive shrinkage estimator for linear panel models that adapts to the amount of information shared between groups. The primary mechanism for the information-sharing is a shrinkage of group-specific distributions towards a new "centroid" distribution through a Kullback-Leibler divergence penalty. The Kullback-Leibler divergence is uniquely geometrically suited for measuring relative information between datasets, and leads to relatively simple closed form estimators with intuitive interpretations. Among other results, we show that our estimator has a provably smaller mean squared error than the group-specific maximum likelihood estimators, and establish asymptotically valid inference procedures. We also propose a new estimator of mean squared error for implementation that leads to improved finite sample performance over minimizing Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE). A comprehensive set of simulations highlights our estimator's versatility, and an analysis of length of stay in ICUs illustrates its performance in a real-world setting.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth M. Davis, Emily C. Hector

item.title: Simplicity Above Elegance: Another Look at the Asymptotically Correct Standardization of Snijders
item.description: arXiv:2605.00216v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Person-fit statistics are widely used to detect aberrant response patterns in educational and psychological measurement. Snijders (2001) suggested an asymptotically correct standardization for a broad class of such statistics. This paper presents an alternative derivation of this standardization. The derivation yields several advantages including a simpler formula and simpler description of several person-fit statistics including the lz* statistic (van Krimpen-Stoop & Meijer, 1999) and a theoretical explanation of simulation findings reported by Snijders (2001) and van Krimpen-Stoop and Meijer (1999), among others.
item.dc:creator: Sandip Sinharay

item.title: 2D Stability Selection: Design Jittering to Exclude Correlated Irrelevant Features
item.description: arXiv:2605.02205v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stability Selection resamples the observations but leaves the design untouched, so it cannot reject an irrelevant feature that is correlated with the relevant ones in a way that violates the irrepresentable condition. Such a feature (a ``confounder'') is selected in a substantial fraction of resamples, and the exchangeability behind the false-positive bound of Stability Selection fails. We propose 2D Stability Selection (2D-SS), which aggregates selection frequencies over half-samples and over a grid of injected design noise, and reduces to Stability Selection at zero noise. Because input noise acts, in expectation, as Tikhonov regularisation, a jittered Lasso fit is a noisy elastic net whose support recovery is governed by a noise-indexed irrepresentable condition. Jittering can therefore repair designs in which confounders violate the Lasso condition, although it can also hurt. We give the noise level at which a violated feature's statistic vanishes (for uncorrelated relevant features), exact-recovery guarantees for a single fit, conditions under which aggregation over noise levels recovers the support, and a complementary-pairs bound on the expected number of false positives, carried over from Stability Selection to the noise-aggregated procedure, for a fixed threshold or a size-matched selector. The procedure takes no measurement-error covariance as input, although the guarantees assume i.i.d.\ Gaussian measurement error. In simulations 2D-SS excludes confounders that Stability Selection includes, and its size-matched version stays below the nominal closed-form false-positive bound in all 240 simulated cells, whereas Stability Selection exceeds it in 21; it does not generally improve on Stability Selection in $F_1$ and is lower at low noise. It is useful when stable but wrong selections are the concern.
item.dc:creator: Mahdi Nouraie, Houying Zhu, Samuel Muller

item.title: Empowering Bayes with sources of uncertainty: from confidence modelling to sparse estimation
item.description: arXiv:2605.03134v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce sources of uncertainty (SoU) inference, a general framework that extends Bayesian inference by allowing researchers to explicitly encode heterogeneous confidence across model components. This heterogeneity allows the probabilistic treatment to vary selectively across the model, controlling both the uncertainty retained within each component and its propagation to the rest of the model. Empirical Bayes and profiling-type inference emerge as limiting configurations of this selective treatment. Because confidence acts through a mechanism distinct from prior informativeness, the two can be controlled separately, providing an additional degree of freedom for Bayesian model design. Building on this selective treatment, we develop a general approach for inducing sparsity in statistical models and illustrate its use in linear and logistic regression, as well as in Bayesian neural networks, where it enables self-pruning.
item.dc:creator: Rafael Mouallem Rosa, Julyan Arbel, Hien Duy Nguyen

item.title: Testing the equality of parameters in fixed and increasing dimension
item.description: arXiv:2607.07588v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper proposes a general and unified framework for testing the equality of a broad class of parameters, defined as a smooth function of expectations of symmetric kernels, across multiple independent populations. We consider two test statistics, a Wald-type statistic and an ANOVA-type statistic. The asymptotic distribution of the first one is derived under a fixed-dimension regime, whereas the second one is studied under both fixed and increasing-dimension regimes, where the parameter dimension diverges with the sample size. Based on these limiting distributions, we construct test procedures enabling asymptotically exact inference without parametric assumptions. Additionally, an alternative null distribution estimator based on a weighted bootstrap approximation is studied, which is applicable to the ANOVA-type statistic under a fixed-dimension regime. The finite-sample performance and computational efficiency of the proposed procedures are evaluated through an extensive simulation study and a real dataset application.
item.dc:creator: M. Romero-Madro\~nal, M. Remedios Sillero-Denamiel, M. Dolores Jim\'enez-Gamero

item.title: Marginal generalized raking with parametric working models
item.description: arXiv:2607.29629v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generalized raking (GR) was originally developed in the survey statistics literature to incorporate auxiliary information in estimation. Recently, it has been used in the biostatistical and epidemiological literature to estimate regression coefficients in parametric models in cases with missing data, including missing data by design (e.g., two-phase studies). In the regression parameter context, the optimal GR estimator has been shown to be equivalent to the optimal augmented inverse probability weighted estimator. In this paper, we generalize the influence function-based theory for GR to marginal estimands; we call our approach marginal generalized raking. We contrast our approach to a procedure that marginalizes a conditional GR estimator of regression parameters; while the former approach is doubly robust, i.e. is consistent if either the missing-data model or the optimal raking variable is estimated consistently, our proposed approach is multiply robust, allowing either the outcome regression or treatment propensity score to also be misspecified. We compare the approaches in both fully-synthetic simulations and in an application using data from an observational cohort of persons living with HIV.
item.dc:creator: Brian D Williamson, Runjia Zou, Thomas Lumley, Bryan E Shepherd, Pamela A Shaw

item.title: Bayesian inference on beta diversity via feature allocation models
item.description: arXiv:2608.11180v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Beta diversity quantifies variation in species composition across ecological communities and is fundamental for understanding biodiversity patterns across space and environmental gradients. Inference is complicated by incomplete sampling, differences among communities and imperfect detection. We develop a partially exchangeable Bayesian feature allocation model for species occurrence data that accommodates unobserved species and incorporates site-specific covariates to relate variation in species composition to environmental conditions. The model yields explicit conditional distributions for species richness and sharing, together with predictions of the species newly recorded at individual sites or newly shared between sites under additional sampling. We also introduce a novel probabilistic beta diversity index with posterior uncertainty quantification. An occupancy--detection representation preserves the tractability of the occurrence model and allows sensitivity analysis under specified detectability assumptions. This tractability makes the approach scalable, enabling inference in large biodiversity studies. Simulation studies assess predictive performance, and an application to global airborne fungal data illustrates how accounting for unobserved species and borrowing information across sites affect inference on compositional heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Federica Stolf, Tommaso Rigon, David B. Dunson

item.title: CVaR anchor regression protects against rare shifts
item.description: arXiv:2609.27034v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study prediction in new environments when the training data contains rare, large distribution shifts. Anchor regression penalizes the average of the squared mean residual across environments. It protects against shifts in an ellipsoid determined by the second moment of the training shifts. Covering rare shifts may therefore require a large penalty $\gamma \gg 1$, expanding the ellipsoid in every direction and reducing accuracy on common environments. We propose CVaR anchor regression, which replaces the average of the squared mean residuals with a tail average. We prove an exact worst-case risk guarantee under a linear structural model that allows for heteroscedastic noise. CVaR anchor regression protects against shifts in a union of ellipsoids determined by second moments of the shifts in the worst $\alpha$-fraction of environments. For $\alpha$ small enough, this is the scaled convex hull of the training shifts and their negatives. It therefore covers all training shifts when $\gamma \geq 1$. Unlike CVaR or GroupDRO applied directly to prediction risks, CVaR anchor regression does not give environments more weight solely because their noise levels are high. Examples show how the method can improve protection against rare shifts while retaining accuracy on common environments. We illustrate the method on the New York City taxi dataset.
item.dc:creator: Malte Londschien

item.title: Identifying compromise solutions across multiple treatment benefit-harm profiles in multivariate network meta-analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.04711v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Health technology assessment often aims to balance evidence across multiple treatments and outcomes and assess treatment benefit-harm profiles. Multivariate network meta-analysis (mvNMA) is well suited to this task, as it synthesizes evidence across treatments and outcomes. However, the potential of mvNMA has been overlooked, leading decision-makers to rely on outcome-specific NMAs that ignore outcome correlations. Based on independent NMA models, previous work proposed methods such as multivariate P-scores or spie charts to assess treatment benefit-harm profiles by yielding across-outcomes treatment hierarchies. In this article, we propose an mvNMA-based framework for assessing treatment benefit-harm profiles. Our framework uses a hybrid-correlation mvNMA model and incorporates DuMouchel priors for treatment effects, enabling estimation of all treatment effects even when outcomes are missing for some treatments. We then extend common NMA ranking metrics, including SUCRA, the probability of being best, and median ranks, to the mvNMA setting. Based on these metrics, we adapt the VIKOR algorithm for mvNMA. This deterministic multicriteria decision method quantifies overall and worst-case treatment performance and, by balancing these aspects, produces an across-outcomes ranking while identifying treatments offering the optimal compromise between these two aspects. To facilitate use of our framework, we developed the R package mvnma. We applied our framework to two clinical datasets: one comparing eleven physical therapy treatments across two outcomes and another comparing nine antidepressants across five outcomes. Our framework provides an alternative strategy for assessing treatment benefit-harm profiles across multiple outcomes and encourages multivariate approaches in applied clinical and policy settings.
item.dc:creator: Theodoros Evrenoglou, Anna Chaimani, Gerta R\"ucker, Guido Schwarzer

item.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14695v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable's entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens. A reanalyzed credit-scoring study shows the cost: a characteristic an optimizing selector uses cannot satisfy exclusion.
item.dc:creator: Michael B\"ucker

item.title: Multiple testing in multi-stream sequential change detection
item.description: arXiv:2501.04130v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-stream sequential change detection involves simultaneously monitoring many data streams and raising an alarm when their distributions change. We study the multiple testing issues that arise naturally in this setting. We first point out a fundamental tension between the criteria used in change detection and multiple testing: any procedure with finite average run length (ARL) must have worst-case false discovery rate (FDR) and family-wise error rate equal to one. Given this conflict, we find a middle ground by introducing the error over patience (EOP) class of Type I error metrics, which measure error relative to expected monitoring time. To control the EOP, we propose procedures combining e-detectors, which generalize Shiryaev-Roberts and CUSUM methods, with the recent e-Benjamini-Hochberg and e-Bonferroni methods for multiple testing. Our EOP guarantees hold uniformly over changepoints and stopping times with finite expectation, allowing dependence when each e-detector remains valid using information from all streams. If finite ARL is forfeited, using e-processes instead yields ordinary FDR and per-family error control at stopping times. We also prove power and delay bounds for Gaussian changes, establish first-order minimax optimality, and compare our procedures with existing methods in numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Sanjit Dandapanthula, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Reliable data clustering with Bayesian community detection
item.description: arXiv:2510.15013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: From neuroscience and genomics to systems biology and ecology, researchers rely on clustering similarity data to uncover modular structure. Most methods work in two steps: first reduce noise, then cluster. The first step runs without regard to the second: it forces arbitrary choices, discards useful information, and can impose structure where none exists. Here we bring the two steps together. Using established Bayesian community detection methods, we let one minimum description length criterion choose both how much to sparsify the data and how to cluster it. This one-step approach keeps all the samples for inference, removes the arbitrary threshold choice, and returns a single cluster when there is no real structure. On synthetic data, our approach recovers clusters under more noise and with fewer samples than standard methods. On gene co-expression data from the human brain, it finds more coherent and more stable clusters than WGCNA, the standard tool in the field. Uniting sparsification and clustering in a single model-selection step provides a principled, noise-resistant way to uncover modular structure in similarity data across fields.
item.dc:creator: Magnus Neuman, Jelena Smiljani\'c, Martin Rosvall

item.title: Rao-Blackwellized e-variables
item.description: arXiv:2512.16759v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that for any concave utility, the expected utility of an e-variable can only increase after conditioning on a sufficient statistic, echoing the classic Rao-Blackwell theorem. The simplest form of the result has a straightforward proof using Jensen's inequality, but we prove more sophisticated versions. We provide several applications of this insight, including a derivation of the log-optimal e-variable for testing the variance in a linear regression model.
item.dc:creator: Dante de Roos, Ben Chugg, Peter Gr\"unwald, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Dyadic Flow Models for Nonstationary Gene Flow in Landscape Genomics
item.description: arXiv:2512.19035v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The field of landscape genomics aims to infer how landscape features affect gene flow throughout a population. Most landscape genomic frameworks assume the isolation-by-distance and isolation-by-resistance hypotheses, which propose that genetic dissimilarities between individuals increase as a function of distance and as a function of cumulative landscape resistance, respectively. While these hypotheses are valid in certain settings, other mechanisms may affect gene flow. For example, the gene flow of invasive species may depend on founder effects and multiple introductions. Such mechanisms are not considered in modern landscape genomic models. We extend dyadic models to allow for mechanisms that range-shifting and/or invasive species may experience by introducing dyadic spatially-varying coefficients (DSVCs) defined on pairs of sampled locations. The DSVCs allow the effects of landscape on gene flow to vary across space, capturing nonstationary and asymmetric connectivity. Additionally, we incorporate explicit landscape features as connectivity covariates, which are localized to specific regions of the spatial domain and may function as barriers or corridors to gene flow. Such covariates are central to colonization and invasion, where spread accelerates along corridors and slows across landscape barriers. The proposed framework accommodates colonization-specific processes while retaining the ability to assess landscape influences on gene flow. Our case study of the highly invasive cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) demonstrates the necessity of accounting for nonstationary gene flow in range-shifting species.
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Schwob, Nicholas M. Calzada, Justin J. Van Ee, Diana Gamba, Rebecca A. Nelson, Megan L. Vahsen, Peter B. Adler, Jesse R. Lasky, Mevin B. Hooten

item.title: A New Family of Poisson Non-negative Matrix Factorization Methods Using the Shifted Log Link
item.description: arXiv:2601.05845v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Poisson non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) is a widely used method to find interpretable "parts-based" decompositions of count data. While many variants of Poisson NMF exist, existing methods assume that the "parts" in the decomposition combine additively. This assumption may be natural in some settings, but not in others. Here we introduce Poisson NMF with the shifted-log link function to relax this assumption. The shifted-log link function has a single tuning parameter, and as this parameter varies the model changes from assuming that parts combine additively (i.e., standard Poisson NMF) to assuming that parts combine more multiplicatively. We provide an algorithm to fit this model by maximum likelihood, and also an approximation that substantially reduces computation time for large, sparse datasets (computations scale with the number of non-zero entries in the data matrix). We illustrate these new methods on a variety of real datasets. Our examples show how the choice of link function in Poisson NMF can substantively impact the results, and how in some settings the use of a shifted-log link function may improve interpretability compared with the standard, additive link.
item.dc:creator: Eric Weine, Peter Carbonetto, Rafael A. Irizarry, Matthew Stephens

item.title: Exploration and Experimentation with a Misspecified Simulator
item.description: arXiv:2605.21458v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Randomized experiments are the standard for measuring causal effects that guide decisions, but are costly. Simulators calibrated to historical data offer a cheaper alternative, but their policies can become suboptimal under drift, a change in dynamics after calibration. We study if, when, and how to collect data for recalibrating the simulator. We consider a system with multiple units running in parallel and managed by a single operator. The real-world system is a partially observed process with a latent variable, while the simulator models it as a fully observed Markovian process, and thus is misspecified. Two data collection strategies exploit the current policy: (i) never recalibrating and (ii) recalibrating from on-policy data (passive adaptation). Two others collect off-policy data by trying actions outside the current policy: (iii) continuous exploration across all units and (iv) randomized experimentation on a sample of units over a predefined window. We investigate these strategies theoretically and in a vending-machine simulation. Experiments can improve on passive adaptation when drift is invisible in on-policy data or recalibration lags behind continuing drift. Experimentation is preferable to exploration when trying a worse action is expensive and the dynamics may not have changed.
item.dc:creator: Harsh Parikh, Gabriel Levin-Konigsberg, Sohrab Andaz, Akhil Bagaria, Dominique Perrault-Joncas, Alexander Volfovsky
